newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Blockbuster troubles roll on as chief leaves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Blockbuster troubles roll on as chief leaves.

text.p: Warning that it expects disappointing results at its Blockbuster Entertainment unit, Viacom Inc. said Tuesday the unit's chairman was resigning and that it will spin off part of the video rental business to the public.
Viacom said Blockbuster Chairman Bill Fields was resigning "by mutual agreement" and a replacement would be named shortly.
The company warned that Blockbuster's performance during the first quarter was likely to fall 15 percent to 20 percent short of its performance a year ago.

In addition Viacom, whose other operations include the Paramount Pictures studio, MTV and other cable TV channels, and publishing, said it will issue a new class of stock which would track the performance of Blockbuster.
Analysts who have been following Viacom's troubles with Blockbuster expressed concern that the latest news indicated the problems were far from over.
"It just questions the company's ability to effectively budget or know what's going on in the business," said Merrill Lynch analyst Jessica Reif.
Viacom's stock was battered after the announcement and closed down $3.375 at $27 a share on the American Stock Exchange.
Fields, a former Wal-Mart Stores executive, joined Blockbuster in March 1996, succeeding Steve Berrard. Viacom bought Blockbuster from founder Wayne Huizenga for $8 billion in 1994.

Fields brought in fresh management and laid plans to deal directly with Hollywood studios on purchasing videos. Plans to move Blockbuster headquarters to Dallas from Fort Lauderdale, Fla., are due to be completed by spring.
He told an investors' meeting in October that Blockbuster aimed to open between 700 and 850 new stores in 1997 while making its existing network more efficient.
Plans also were made to develop "entertainment centers" offering a diverse variety of products.
"Bill Fields was presented as the savior. Now the savior is dead. He fell on his sword," said Josephthal Lyon & Ross analyst Dennis McAlpine.
Several analysts said they were concerned that it will likely take Fields' successor at least 12 months to get up to speed with the unit's operations, potentially stalling any turnaround.
A Viacom spokeswoman said plans for the retail complexes were still going forward. The first Viacom Entertainment Store is due to open in Chicago next month.
"It's a Viacom initiative. The executives in charge are still there. It's still very much on track," spokeswoman Susan Duffy said.
Viacom said in a statement the unit's poor results were brought on by "the inferior quality of video releases in the period" and the short term costs related to its decision to move its headquarters.
The new stock issue will track Blockbuster's performance and while it will make the stock available to the investors in a public offering, Viacom will retain a majority of the shares.

"Issuing a tracking stock will enable us to raise equity capital to reduce our debt, will provide an attractive opportunity for investors interested in Blockbuster and will make it possible for shareholders to better capture the value of all of Viacom's businesses," Chairman Sumner Redstone said.

At the end of 1996 Blockbuster had more than 5,300 domestic and international video stores in 24 countries and about 500 music stores. Its video and music store operations had 1996 revenues of $3.54 billion.
Blockbuster has been a difficult segment for Viacom as the cable and satellite industries cut into the video retailing.
Viacom has about $9.9 billion in debt, Duffy said. Its planned sale of 10 radio stations is expected to lower the debt by between $700 million and $800 million.
Viacom repeated its goal to lower debt to between $6 billion and $8 billion by the end of 1999.

Blockbuster operations reported revenues of $3.54 billion and earnings before taxes, interest and other items of $775 million in 1996. For 1996, Viacom reported revenues of $12.08 billion and earnings before taxes of $2.09 billion.
